• Measurements made at four locations over the last few decades show that pH has decreased consistently, which means acidity has increased. This increase in acidity coincides with higher levels of dissolved carbon dioxide.
  • Ocean pH is projected to continue to decrease under all four emissions scenarios during the next several decades. Modeled ranges suggest that pH could stabilize or begin to recover during the last few decades of this century under the low emissions scenario, where there are significant reductions in greenhouse gas and other air pollutant emissions. Acidity will continue to increase under the other three scenarios, however.
  • Under the very high emissions scenario, pH is projected to decrease from about 8.1 historically to about 7.7 in 2100. A change this large will present serious challenges to many organisms that build shells or skeletons from calcium carbonate, as it would require them to use more energy to extract that carbonate from the water. The low emissions scenario would avoid this impact.[1]
